en: *Commentary on the Sutra of the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara: Elucidating the Meaning*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang during the Song Dynasty.

Regarding the four characters “Sutra of the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara,” they constitute the specific title of this commentary (*shu*). “Commentary” (*shu*) is the general term, used because it provides an explanation.
Because this work serves as a general commentary (*śāstra*) on various sutras, it is distinguished from them by briefly indicating these four characters.
"Commentary" (*shu*) means to "unravel" (*shu*) and to "decide" (*jue*).
It unravels the principles of the sutra texts and decides upon their meanings and purports.

However, when the wise explain a sutra, they designate the interpretation of the title as the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and the interpretation of the text as the *Wenju* (Textual Phrases); when the *Xuanyu* and *Wenju* are combined into a single work, it is titled a *Shu* (Commentary).
Since these two now coincide, I have thus titled this commentary [“Sūtra Commentary”].
“Tiantai” refers to the mountain where he resided;
“Zhizhe” refers to the person who was able to expound the teachings.

Formerly, when Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty was still the Prince of Jin, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Great Master; subsequently, following the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, he established a title for his teacher, naming him "The Wise One" (Zhìzhě).
Regarding the term "Great Master" (*Mahāśāstrin*): "Great" is a word of praise and commendation; "Master" is a title for one who teaches others the Way.
In antiquity, if one's understanding or practice served as a model for others, people would invariably refer to them as a "Great Master."
During the reign of Emperor Yizong of the Tang dynasty, he was appointed to serve as an Acting Official; from that time onward, although the position existed in name, no one dared to summon him.
As for the term "shuo" (exposition), it refers to engaging in free-flowing debate and discourse, rather than the composition of written works.
Since these writings were recorded by the disciple Zhān'ān, he did not record the Master’s taboo names but instead inscribed his honorific titles. As for the term "disciple" (dìzǐ):
in terms of resources, he abandoned his father to follow his teacher and revered his teacher as a father;
yet, out of the teacher's humility and courtesy, he was treated as a younger brother (dì) by his teacher.
Thus we know that the name "disciple" (dizi) is imbued with reverence and deference.
Therefore, when a teacher summons a student to be his disciple, it lies in the virtue of yielding;
when the student likewise refers to himself as a disciple, it lies in the virtue of reverence.
Although there are differing accounts, I shall now rely on the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra).
As for the "Master Ding," his taboo name was Guanding and his courtesy name was Fayun; he was a native of Zhang’an in Linhai.
As for the Master Yunding, this commentary originally contained no title for its author; it was later described by subsequent generations.
Therefore, his personal name is not recorded, which is in accordance with the rules of propriety.
As for the *Dharma-paryāya-vidhi* and the *Dharmadhātu-anupūrvi*, since they were personally composed by the Great Master, he inscribed his own name and title therein.
As for the various other sections, whenever a disciple recorded his words, it was always stated simply that "the Dharma Master Zhizhe spoke thus."
Furthermore, as with the *Nirvāṇa Commentary*, since it was edited and finalized by Jingxi, it likewise bears the inscription "Compiled by Dharma Master Ding.
This serves as a model; those who follow should take it as their standard.

The *Book of Rites* states, "One does not avoid [the pronunciation of] individual characters in a two-character name," meaning that one need not avoid pronouncing each character of a two-character name individually; therefore, we now refer to it as "Ding" (Crown) rather than "Guan" (Consecration).
Furthermore, regarding the Master’s taboo name Zhìyǐ, which is now referred to as "Zhìzhě" (the Wise One), it is merely a matter of avoiding one character.
To avoid the entire name was not the ancient practice; it is merely a regulation of later generations.
That being so, one does not avoid taboo characters when dealing with the *Shi* and *Shu*, nor does one avoid them when reading the texts; since the lecturer cites them in full, there is no fault.
The *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of five kinds of Dharma-preachers:
first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing.
Now, Zhang’an is precisely the person who provides the exegesis; therefore, people have summoned him to serve as Dharma Master.
As for "Records" (*ji*), it means recording the words of the Master.
Next, we enter the text.
The following section, as its commentary has already been circulated separately, is no longer included here.
Regarding the "Person and the Dharma": one should invoke Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; this refers to the person.
The *Dhāraṇī for Eliminating and Subduing Poisonous Harm* is the Dharma.

If one considers it from the perspective of one's own practice, the Dharma should come first and the person second; this is because the Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher, and Avalokiteśvara attained the Way through his realization of the Dharma.
Now, in accordance with the purpose of transforming others, the person is mentioned first and the Dharma second; for the Dharma does not operate in isolation, but is propagated through people.
Since Avalokiteśvara explains the Dharma he has realized to cure the poison of the three obstacles of others, the title of the sutra places the person before the Dharma.
"Below 'human' is the objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*); as it transcends the laws of birth and death, it is called ultimate compassion (*parama-maitrī*).
Because its Way surpasses that of ordinary beings and the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), he is termed a Great Being (*mahāsattva*).
Because he is free from the evils of the two extremes (*antadvaya*), he is called supremely virtuous."
Because its efficacy in subduing obstacles is never in vain, it is called a "divine mantra" (shenzhou).

The "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) is the one who speaks it, and the "divine mantra" is the Dharma that is spoken. "Supreme compassion" reveals the virtue of the Great Being, while "supreme goodness" praises the merit of the divine mantra.
The "multitude of capacities" refers to Candraprabha and the people of Vaiśālī.
Regarding the capacity as the subject that responds: if the multitude of capacities is taken as the one who can evoke, then Avalokiteśvara is the one who is evoked;
if Avalokiteśvara is taken as the one who can respond, then the multitude of capacities is the one who is responded to.

Now, that which is moved by the Sage is designated as the "responsive capacity" (nengying), while that which responds to the ordinary person is designated as the "moving capacity" (nenggian); each is named according to its functional power.

Thus we know that the ordinary person is able to move because they are endowed with the three thousand [dharmas] by principle (liju), whereas the Sage is able to respond because the three thousand are partially manifested (fenshan).
Regarding the phrase "extinguishing and subduing" (*xiāofú*) and so forth: "extinguishing" (*xiāo*) means to eliminate; "subduing" (*fú*) means to tame.
The three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) are collectively termed "poisonous harms.
As the Sūtra says: "By eliminating the three obstructions, one is free from all malevolent powers."
This is precisely its function.
Furthermore, it is called "power" because it generates goodness, and it is called "function" because it eliminates evil.
This mantra eliminates the three obstructions; this is its function.
The manifestation of the three truths is its power.
"True essence" refers to the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "in this land" and so forth: since *dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term, it is translated here in this region as "retention" (*zhuchi*).
The "three meanings" refer to upholding the name, upholding the practice, and upholding the meaning.
The "two extremes" refer to birth-and-death and nirvana.
Therefore, one should know that the principle of the three virtues is such that, being quiescent yet illuminating, it is able to uphold; being illuminating yet quiescent, it is able to exclude.
Below the phrase "As for 'using' (*yòng jí*)," this commentary provides three successive expositions of the title, each discussing three points:
first, the person who preaches; second, the Dharma being preached; and third, the general title of the sutra.
The person and the general title are distinguished below.
The Dharma has three meanings, which are precisely addressed in this passage; therefore, in the specific explanation that follows, they are simply explained as they are.
That the general and specific texts mutually manifest their meanings reflects both the Master’s skill in preaching the Dharma and the elegance of Zhiyi’s (Chang’an) penmanship.

However, while this section now encompasses all four teachings, the three successive phases and their three meanings are all discussed in terms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). This is because it is the intended purport of the text, because it pertains to the gate of practice, because the profound includes the shallow, and because it represents the Buddha’s original intent. Therefore, both the speaker and the listener should carefully deliberate upon this.
Regarding the phrase "As for the matters," the following three passages all directly demonstrate poisons and harms in order to manifest their subjugation and pacification.

As for "tigers, wolves," and so forth, this refers to what the Sūtra says: "If one encounters tigers, wolves, lions, as well as poisonous drugs, swords, or blades, or when facing execution, by invoking my name and reciting this dhāraṇī, one shall attain liberation. All of these concern the subjugation and pacification of actual phenomena.

The "five abodes" refer to taking the afflictions of the three realms of seeing as one, and the afflictions of the three realms of thought as three; together with fundamental ignorance, these constitute five.

Because they are all states of delusion and vexation that disturb and confuse the nature of the mind, they are collectively termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*); thus, these afflictions are metaphorically named after tigers, wolves, and the like.
The Sūtra states, "Purify the roots of the three poisons so as not to be afflicted by the three poisons," which serves as clear evidence regarding the practice.

Therefore, when the sub-commentary below explains the tigers and wolves, it cites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* on how even those in the tenth stage may still encounter the perils of tigers and wolves; this is precisely that meaning.
Cultivating the threefold contemplation within a single mind to destroy the delusions of the five abodes is precisely the purification of practice.

As for "the non-obstruction of the dharma-realm": the single mind of the three truths is called the dharma-realm; because sentient beings and Buddhas are mutually interfused and each and every thing is omnipresent, it is termed "non-obstructive."

Regarding "being unstained yet stained," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "The self-nature of the Middle Way, the intrinsically pure mind, is not defiled by afflictions; it is fundamentally neither bound nor liberated. That it is 'unstained yet stained' is difficult to comprehend."
This refers to sentient beings who, being deluded regarding the true nature of liberation, give rise to the sixty-two views.
Examining the meaning of those words, they accord perfectly with the present text.
To interpret the present text, one should say that *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and ignorance together pervasively create all dharmas; thus, there is non-defilement within defilement.
When the entirety of principle (*li*) becomes poison, it is called "the poison of principle.
Because of this poison of principle, there arise the poisons of practice (*xing*) and phenomena (*shi*).
Now, observing that all dharmas are mind-only and that the essence of defilement is entirely pure, one employs the divine mantra to treat the poison of principle.
This refers to what the sutra below states: "All enter the limit of reality as it is.
If this is so, how does this differ from [the classification] based on practice?
Answer:
The previous reference to "practitioner" (xingzhe) was made in terms of wisdom and abandonment (*jueduan*):
wisdom is that which abandons, while abandonment is that which is abandoned; the state where the five abodes (*wuzhu*) are abandoned is called "dissolving the poison of practice.
Now, however, it is not so; this refers exclusively to the principle of the Truths (*di li*).
In principle, there is neither subject nor object; it is simply that because one possesses afflictions (*kleśa*), one is "stained while being unstained," which is termed "poisonous harm.
Afflictions are themselves the *dharmatā*; thus, they are "stained while being unstained," which is termed "subduing and eliminating."
This implies that the nature of delusion is mutually dependent and does not pertain to the severance by wisdom.
Alternatively, if it is claimed that the evil nature is the "poison of principle," then while the meaning of "poison" may be established, the meaning of "elimination" is entirely absent.
If there were no meaning of "dissolving," how could it be called a function?
If you say that there is, then the inherent evil (xing-è) should be destroyed;
yet the dharma-gate of inherent evil is indestructible.
Regarding the phrase "The five layers," the subsequent notes and so forth need no further elaboration;
first, they are listed.
From the words "As for 'names,'" the five chapters are explained and demonstrated.

Now, regarding the "Explanation of Names" (*Shiming*), it provides a general discussion on the essence, substance, and function of the three dharmas, and a specific discussion on the pedagogical characteristics and distinctions of those same three dharmas.

As for the statement that "persons and dharmas constitute the names," *Qing* is the one who initiates the response and *Guanyin* is the one who responds; this refers to the substance of resonance and response.
To eliminate and subdue poisonous harms is to clarify their functional power; this is the function of rescuing those in peril and uprooting suffering.
*Dhāraṇī* clarifies their essential substance; this is the *dharmakāya*.
This is where the general discussion of the "Explanation of Names" lies.

Regarding the statement that "supreme spiritual awareness is the essence," while the sutras encompass all four teachings and their principles vary between partial and perfect, if one discusses the true essence, one takes only the perfect principle.

Spiritual awareness, quiescence, and illumination are all the Dharmakāya; this is the meaning of "illumination. Nevertheless, although quiescence and illumination are non-dual, since the Bodhisattva is designated by name according to their contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), and because the designation follows the capacity [of that wisdom], the meaning of "illumination" is taken as the essence.
To illustrate this by way of example: if one names it "cessation-concentration" (*śamatha*), its essence should be taken as the meaning of quiescence.

The numinous awareness is precisely the Dharmakāya—the numinous, luminous, and fundamentally awakened state. What is called "quiescent illumination" refers to this numinous awareness; it is the Dharmakāya being illuminated while remaining in a state of quiescence.
One should know that the three bodies are all eternal and the three truths are simultaneously illumined; yet, following the preeminent and the fundamental, we provisionally designate the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, their essential nature is originally one, though they possess various names; thus, while the various scriptures clarify the essence, the names differ according to the specific texts and their respective meanings.
The *Lotus Sūtra* primarily concerns the revelation of the provisional, taking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.
Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* demonstrates final extinction, it takes the nirvāṇa of inherent purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*) as its essence.
In the "Universal Gate" [chapter], having already discussed the two bodies, it takes the numinous wisdom as the essence that accords with the Dharma-body.
This numinous wisdom is the Reward-body; by uniting the Reward-body with the Dharma-body, the meaning of the two bodies is clarified as being the True Body.
As for this present sutra, since the descent of the three sages already manifests the three virtues, the Dharma-body is established as the essence (*tattva*) of the sutra.

Furthermore, while the "Universal Gate" chapter clarifies the manifestation of forms according to various types of beings, this sutra clarifies the arrival of the Holy Lord; because the meaning of the body (*kāya*) is more convenient in this context, the name "body" is established for both when distinguishing the essence.

Regarding the phrase "taking resonance and response as the core principle": the offering of the request by Yuegai constitutes the "stimulus" (gan), while the distant descent of the Three Sages constitutes the "response" (ying). Since the arising of the teaching originates from this, it is taken as the core principle.
However, while various sutras may take cause and effect as their primary theme, such an approach is not convenient for clarifying the meaning of this present sutra.
Why is this? Because the terminology of "cause and effect" is general, applying to both ordinary beings and sages alike.
For example, when an ordinary person makes a request for rescue as the cause and later attains the Way as the result, this is the causality of ordinary beings.
When Avalokiteśvara was formerly at the stage of an ordinary being as the cause and now dwells in partial realization as the result, this is the causality of sages.
Now, although ordinary beings possess both cause and effect, they are designated by the term "stimulus" (gan);
although sages possess both cause and effect, they are designated by the term "response" (ying). Therefore, the central tenet is that of stimulus and response.

Regarding the phrase "its function is to rescue from peril and extract from suffering": because it causes one to abandon the peril of illness and suffering—which is like being suspended upside down—it rescues and extracts them through great compassion so that they are restored to their original state. Although it also bestows happiness, extracting from suffering is its primary purpose.

Regarding the phrase "The Mahāyāna as the characteristic of the teaching": "Great" (mahā) signifies inclusion; "vehicle" (yāna) signifies that which carries one across. "Teaching" (jiao) refers to the words of the Sage directed toward those below; "characteristic" (xiang) refers to the differentiation of similarities and differences.
Although this school discusses the four teachings, its primary intent lies in the Mahāyāna of the three [lower] teachings.
Regarding the phrase "distinguishing by means of the three meanings," these three meanings encompass everything when considered in terms of the beginning and end of spiritual practice.

This means that by practicing in accordance with the teachings, one's practice accords with the principle; because these three meanings possess both general and specific aspects, they are designated as "general" and "specific.
These three constitute the essential purport of the two designations, general and specific.
If categorized by stage, it belongs to the stage of "names" (nāmamātra) in terms of the teaching, because one receives the teaching and gives rise to understanding;
it belongs to the stages of "contemplative practice" (pratipatti) and "conformity" (sādṛśya) in terms of practice, because one practices based on that understanding;
and it resides in the first dwelling (prathamabhūmi) in terms of principle, because one partially realizes the fundamental principle.

Nevertheless, regarding the stage of practice, one must proceed with composure; if one is merely engaged in cultivation while still abiding at the level of names and concepts, it is not yet called "contemplative practice" (vipaśyanā-caryā), for that name is applied only when the practice is definitively realized.
Whenever one examines the stages of progress, this principle must be understood.
The section beginning with "The Teacher" explains these three meanings.

In terms of both principle (li) and practice (xing), they are categorized as general and specific; while the specific practices correspond to the rational nature (lixing), they all ultimately converge in the single principle despite having different names. Only the first [category], which concerns the teaching (jiao), does not correlate with principle to clarify its meaning.
Regarding the term "śrāvaka" (voice-hearer):
"voice" refers to the sound that is heard;
"teaching" refers to the eight qualities of voice and the four analytical knowledges.
"Hearing" refers to the faculty capable of hearing, which employs the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) to grasp and discriminate.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The ear-faculty is unimpaired, and the sound is within the range of audibility."
Since the capacities [of sentient beings] differ, what is taught differs;
since what is taught differs, the various sections (nikāyas) become distinct.
Because each of these sūtras has its own specific name, it is said that "the names differ."
"Other disciples" refers to the noble ones of the three vehicles.
Question:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that "Buddhist scriptures are spoken by four types of persons: namely, disciples, various sages, various devas, and emanated beings."
"Now, why do you say it is not so?
He replied:
"Because it was approved by the Buddha, it is equally designated as the Buddha's teaching."

Now, in this sutra, when Avalokiteśvara speaks the dhāraṇī and Śāriputra explains that the four great elements equally enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), they are all termed "the Buddha’s teaching" because they bear the seal of the Buddha.
As for the phrase "many paths to enter the Way," the ultimate principle is empty and pervasive; it is designated as the "Way."
The various sutras speak of the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold teachings) to demonstrate the paths for entering into principle; since these are not of a single type, they are said to have "many routes.

Regarding the phrase "differences in the gates of contemplation": for example, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the four practices of peace and bliss serve as the gate for entering into principle, whereas in the present sutra, methods such as counting the breath (*ānāpāna*) serve as the gate for entering into principle.
Furthermore, the four teachings and four gates differ from one another, all of which constitute distinct doctrines.
"Attuning to the Way" means attaining and uniting with the true Way; it refers to the moment of entering the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) and partially realizing the three virtues (*tri-dharma*).
Upon reaching this stage, cultivation and nature are unified as one without further differentiation; hence it is said, "they together return to a single principle.
"Principle" refers precisely to the principle realized within the aforementioned gate of contemplation.
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) means that its essence is not false or deceptive; therefore, it is called "true nature.
Because it is without change or alteration, it is termed "such" (*tathā*).
Because its name corresponds to reality and is not empty, it is called the "ultimate limit" (*koṭi*).
Because it is neither the characteristic of birth-and-death nor the characteristic of nirvana, it is called the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

"Ālaya"—also *ālayavijñāna*—is here translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*cangshi*), because it can store its own substance within all phenomena, and store all phenomena within its own substance.
These are all different terms for the single mind’s three truths.
Question:
Why is the ninth pure consciousness not used as a designation for the principle?
Answer:
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the Master explains that the ālayavijñāna is a truly permanent and pure consciousness, and thus does not establish a ninth consciousness;

however, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the ālaya is a neutral consciousness associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance, and it is only when it is transformed that it is called "pure."
Thus we know that these two treatises differ according to their adaptation to the capacities of beings.
If one proceeds from the perspective of identity (*ji*), it reaches only up to the eighth stage, where it still says that "ignorance itself is the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
If one proceeds from the perspective of separation (*li*), the ninth stage is established, where it says that "the severing of ignorance is itself the dharma-nature."

If one understands the present school, it follows logically that there should be no dispute: they are neither identical nor separate, for their single essence is without distinction; yet, being both identical and separate, why should these two standpoints not coexist?
The analogy of waves and water makes this general principle clear.
The section beginning with "The Dharma of Humans" clarifies the purpose of the discourse.
*Dhāraṇī* refers to the three virtues, which are the dharmas realized;
*Avalokiteśvara* refers to the person who realizes them.
Having personally realized the three virtues, I now recite this dharani so that others may likewise realize them.
Thus, the Dharma relies on the person for its propagation, and the person is established through the Dharma; they are mutually supportive and identical, inseparable even for a moment.
Now, following the title of the sutra and focusing on the meaning of transforming others, the person is presented first and the dharma second.

As for "requesting by oneself," this refers to Śāriputra’s inquiry regarding the coordination of faculties and objects and their inclusion within the meditative absorptions; since he sought this for his own entry into the Way, it is called "requesting by oneself."
Candracchattra [requested this] for the sake of curing the grave illness of Śrīgarbha; thus, it was for the benefit of others.
The Buddha spoke these verses as an entrustment for their circulation in order to protect the True Dharma.
These three types are all called "Invocations to Avalokiteśvara."
If one were to follow the sequence of the scriptural text, the practice for the sake of others would come first.

However, here we prioritize logical convenience; therefore, we list the practice for oneself first. This is because the intention behind practicing for oneself is narrow, that for the sake of others is broader, and the protection of the Dharma is the broadest. Thus, they are arranged in order from the narrow to the broad.
Question:

When Srona requested [the teaching] and Śāriputra spoke of the six sense faculties, and the Tathāgata entrusted [the Dharma] to the eight classes of beings, why is it called the "Request of Avalokiteśvara"?
Answer:
Avalokiteśvara descended from afar with the intention of expounding the methods for subduing obstacles.
That which Subhūti requested was likewise for this purpose.
The Tathāgata’s entrustment to the eight classes of beings was also solely to ensure that these methods endure in the world for a long time.
Although the individuals addressed differ, the Dharma-gates are no different; since the Dharma is used to manifest the person, all are invocations of Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding the three invocations, they correspond respectively to the three aggregates of precepts: the first should be paired with the aggregate of morality (saṃvara-śīla), and the third with the aggregate of gathering wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla).
The *Sūtra of the Adornment* states: "The precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the ten *pārājikas*.
The *Commentary on the Precepts* states: "The restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-saṃgraha*) is able to cause the mind to abide [in stability]."
This accords with the meaning of Sona’s own request.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states: “The gathering of wholesome dharmas refers to the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
The *Commentary on the Precepts* (Jièshù) states: “Gathering wholesome dharmas means that one spontaneously accomplishes the Buddha-dharmas.”
This corresponds to the request for the Tathāgata to protect the Dharma.

The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* states: "Gathering in sentient beings refers to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it means transforming sentient beings so that they may attain peace and happiness."
The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: “‘Gathering beings’ means to bring sentient beings to maturity.
This corresponds to the request made by Candracchattra on behalf of others.
Therefore, the three requests in this sutra constitute the three clusters (*triskandha*).
These names for the three aggregates appear in the *Vaipulya* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

As for the text stating, "Voluntarily requesting [teachings] is the aggregate of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*), and protecting the Dharma is the aggregate of gathering the true Dharma (*saddharma-saṃgrāhaka*)," this may be a textual error, or it may be based on a separate source.
The passage beginning with "If one attains" below demonstrates the integration of the three fundamental precepts (*śīla-mūla*).
Since the preceding text already addressed the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), here it specifically reconciles two of those names.

Furthermore, there may be a textual error; it should rather state: "The clarity and purity of one's own ethical discipline (*śīla*) is itself the restraint of the code (*saṃvara-śīla*); the clarity and purity of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*)."
"Clarity and purity" refers to the stage of partial conformity to truth (*samyaktva-nyāma*), and its meaning also extends to the stage of contemplative practice (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the citation from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: all phenomena are mind-only; thus, the three—precept, concentration, and wisdom—are fully present within the mind itself.
Since my own mind is thus, so it is with all Buddhas; because self and other are mutually interfused, there is no distinction.

Because there is no distinction, the Buddha reveals what he has realized to me; since my own mind is now pure, I am likewise able to transform others. Thus the meaning of the three clusters (triskandha) becomes manifest, and one finally understands that the essence of the three requests is fundamentally interfused.

Regarding the phrase "the two attendants" and so forth: one's own practice is the primary [standard], while others such as Śrīkṣānti, Candracchattra, and Dharmapāla serve as secondary standards. When discussing these primary and secondary standards in relation to the Tathāgata, one must certainly provide three requests.
Practitioners of future generations should take this as their model for emulation.
"To cause" (zhì) means to reach;
"to pray" (qí) means to announce.
"Qian" means "to seek.
Regarding "the essential mind," "essential" refers to a solemn vow; both of these are derived from the citations provided below.

Since the preceding section has already clarified the self-petition, it would have been appropriate to cite the petition of Śīlabhadra; however, the petition of Candracchattra was cited because its text is explicit and easy to understand.
Discussing them from both collateral and primary perspectives, the three requests are mutually complete and mutually cited, without being confined by boundaries.
The intent of the boundaries is that the specific request pertains exclusively to Avalokiteśvara and does not apply to other sages.

Regarding "inviting through practice": although one does not explicitly set the intention, because one's conduct is pure, one naturally attains the state of a sage; thus, the purity of conduct itself constitutes the invitation, and it is therefore called "inviting through practice."
The same applies to the request for realization.
Regarding "Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi," as described in the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*, when the samādhi is accomplished, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in the air and so forth.
In essence, although the words do not explicitly mention the mind, when one realizes the principle, one naturally beholds Avalokiteśvara.

The stage of practice for requesting [protection] lies within the contemplative practices (*guanxing*); the stage of realization for requesting [protection] lies within the six sense faculties and the first stage of dwelling (*chuzhu*).
Regarding the "focusing of the mind," the first point means that its stages encompass both the profound and the shallow.
Under the heading "bodily action" (*kāyakarman*), the text provides examples showing that verbal and mental actions each likewise possess three types of requests.
Although the preceding passage spoke of the "three actions being without flaw," it was specifically referring to bodily action.
Question:
It may be that the body acts erroneously due to verbal karma; however, why is it said that mental karma is characterized by the mind and so forth?
Answer:
If one follows this present sutra, observing the mind, the heart-veins, and the [visualized] image leads to seeing Avalokiteśvara; this is the invocation of the mind (*citta*).

If one follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, wherein one simply observes the true reality (*tathatā*) of the nature of the mind and sees Avalokiteśvara spontaneously upon entering the stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), then since the mind was not initially invoked, this constitutes the invocation through practice (*pratipatti*) and the invocation through realization (*adhigama*).
However, these requests in the treatise all refer to perceiving his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If it is marked that the mind has no resonance, this is due to the shallowness of past and present conditions, and does not pertain to the meaning of the present request.
To be moved without being signaled arises from the profound conditions of the past and present; this is the meaning of the current request.
That the mind is further moved by signaling can be understood through its underlying principle.
As it is with this Sage, so it is with all other Sages.

Furthermore, among the three karmas of sentient beings, some are stronger than others; where a karma is strong, it can serve as the "trigger" (ki). Therefore, regarding each of the three karmas, three types of requests are discussed.

As for the phrase "adding twelve to the previous," this refers to the three categories of self-benefit, benefiting others, and protecting the Dharma, each possessing the three modes of prolonging, entreating, and aspiring—thus totaling twelve.
Question:
Since the protection of the Dharma is that which the Tathāgata entrusted [to us], why is it also discussed in terms of the three karmas, such as the invocation of the mind and so forth?
Answer:
Although the sutras contain such entrustments, do practitioners not likewise invoke Avalokiteśvara for the sake of protecting the True Dharma?

Regarding the "Invocation according to the Nine Realms," even Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles must invoke the Avalokiteśvara of the Perfect Teaching in order to eliminate the three obstacles that lie beyond their respective realms.
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha-realm must be carefully discerned," one should ask:
"While this may be so for the nine realms, how should one request [the Dharma] regarding the Buddha-realm?
One should answer:

Name and contemplative practice are themselves the Buddha; for the sake of eliminating the three obstacles of the fragmented [birth-and-death], one must request the Avalokiteśvara of partial realization.
It is likewise for the sake of eliminating the three obstacles of the transformative [birth-and-death] that the Buddha of semblance is invoked.

Within the stage of partial realization, each level acts upon the others, continuing until the stage of Equal Enlightenment; at this point, one requests the ultimate Avalokiteśvara to eliminate the three obstacles.
This refers to the fivefold "identicalities" within the Perfect Teaching, all of which are designated as the Buddha-realm.
If one takes the ultimate stage as the requester, it is because sentient beings' capacity to sever evil resides in Avalokiteśvara; therefore, he must be invoked.
This is as the sutra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and to protect all, again entreated the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "Bodhisattvas are all endowed with manifold virtues": they are endowed with manifold virtues because they have perfectly realized the true principle (*tattva*).

Mañjuśrī—whose full name is Mañjuśrī—is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*). Because he perceives the Buddha-nature of the three virtues as neither vertical nor horizontal, he is called Wondrous Virtue.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "To see the Buddha-nature clearly is to be like Miaode (Sudhana) and others.
Maitreya is here translated as Cishi (the Benevolent One). As his single essence comprises the three types of compassion, encompassing all that exists, this became his name.

In the section following "The Ultimate Discourse" (*Zhilun*), it is clarified that the essential nature is fundamentally integrated, thereby explaining the meaning that all [qualities] are fully endowed with manifold virtues.
Therefore, virtue, compassion, and wisdom—these three—are one essence with different names, mutually encompassing one another.

Because the three virtues, the three types of compassion, and the three types of wisdom are non-different in essence, the "objectless" [wisdom] and the "knowledge of all modes" are both designated according to their predominant aspects; in their central essence, they simultaneously illumine both, such that compassion and wisdom are each complete in all three.
The phrase "But according to [the occasion]" (*dàn dòu*) below clarifies that titles are established in accordance with the capacities of beings.
For those who are suitable to hear [a teaching], there are four types of benefit (*siddhi*) according to what they hear; therefore, each is given a distinct title.
“Being the same in terms of the causal ground” means they share the same true cause.
Regarding “each explaining the cause of the body,” the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 32, states: “Five hundred bhikṣus asked Śāriputra:
‘The Buddha has spoken of the cause of the body; what is it?’”
Śāriputra replied:
"Each of you has likewise attained right liberation; you should know this for yourselves.
For what reason, then, do you ask such a question?"
A bhikṣu said:
"When we had not yet attained right liberation, we thought that ignorance was the cause of the body.
When we practiced this contemplation, we attained the fruit of arhatship."
Some spoke of craving, some spoke of volitional formations, and so on, up to food, drink, and the five objects of desire.
Thus these five hundred went together to the Buddha’s presence and each declared that they had attained understanding.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying, "Who speaks correctly?
The Buddha replied:
"Nothing is not the correct teaching.
Regarding the "thirty-two," at the beginning of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the Bodhisattva Dharmavimati said:
"Arising and ceasing are two; non-arising and non-ceasing are non-dual."
...and so on, until Mañjuśrī says:
"Non-explanation and non-demonstration constitute entry into non-duality.
Together, there are thirty-two persons.
If the lay practitioners (gṛhapati) are included, there are thirty-three.
Regarding the phrase "entering together" (*tóng rù*) below: although the five hundred bhikṣus and the four great bodhisattvas differ in their modes of entry, that which they enter is no different.
Speaking in terms of crossing the boundaries between stages, the five hundred destinies are indeed real.
For example, the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "The four times four make sixteen, all of which share the same destination of eternal bliss."
"Single principle" means that although the myriad dharmas differ, the nature of the mind is eternally one; hence it is called the "single principle.
"Yet they are also different" refers to the distinctness of their meanings and purposes.
Thus, although the essence of the principle is the same, its meanings differ and its names differ.
Because the principle possesses the meaning of universal illumination, it is given the name "contemplative wisdom" (guan-zhi);
because the principle possesses the meaning of universal inclusion, it is given the title "Maitreya" (Ci-shi).
Although the names and meanings differ, they constitute but a single principle; therefore, it is said that "one does not depart from the principle.
In explaining the specific names, one should first divide the section into two parts:
first, explaining "response" (*ying*) in terms of object and wisdom; second, explaining "capacity" (*ji*) in terms of realms and karma.

Regarding the general and specific explanations: the general explanation involves the combined analysis of object and wisdom, while the specific explanation involves the separate exposition of object and wisdom.

As for the terms "refutation" and "establishment": the names of the contemplations are fundamentally the inconceivable object and wisdom beyond the triple world; yet, in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, they are also treated as conceivable object and wisdom—both of which transcend the four propositions and are free from the hundred deliberations.
People give rise to four kinds of attachment to natures regarding this; therefore, one must first refute these four attachments.

Once the four have been refuted and all are encompassed by the objects, then the objects and wisdom of the *garbha* (storehouse) are established, eventually leading to the establishment of the objects and wisdom of the Perfect [Teaching]; thus, they must be established subsequently.
Regarding the section beginning with "The refuter" (*bhettṛ*), first the names of the objects and the cognition are established as the targets of refutation.
"The world" (*loka*) refers to the threefold world.
Regarding the section beginning with "Now I ask," there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for each when comparing the object and the cognition; these can be understood from the text itself.
Regarding the phrase "the object is an object by itself," etc., it means that the object is inherently an object and cognition is inherently cognition; they do not depend upon one another.

As for the statement "this arises from itself": if one says that the object is inherently an object, then the object does not depend on the illumination of cognition to be an object—it is an object that arises from itself.

If it is claimed that cognition is inherently cognition and does not arise dependent upon an object, such that this cognition arises spontaneously—here, only the first clause is challenged, while the remaining three are treated by analogy; hence the term "and so forth" (etc. is used.
If one wishes to prepare for the objection, the subsequent lines should state: "If cognition arises because of the object, then that cognition is produced by another;
if the object arises because of cognition, then that object is produced by another."
Why is this? Because it is its own object, it is called an "object"; yet, since the object is designated as "self," when the object is viewed from the perspective of wisdom, that wisdom is "other.
Now, if the object arises from wisdom, how could it not be an "other-object"?

Wisdom is also like this. If an object exists because it is conjoined with wisdom, and wisdom exists because it is conjoined with an object, then this object does not exist as an object by virtue of wisdom, nor does it exist as an object by virtue of itself; rather, the object exists because the conditions of wisdom and the object are in harmony. Wisdom is also like this.
This is co-arising; co-arising entails two faults, as it falls into the categories of self-nature and other-nature.

If it is claimed that "neither wisdom nor object exists, yet because there is an object there is wisdom," this would mean that object and wisdom are distinguished without an object, without wisdom, and without any causal conditions.
Since even that which arises from causes and conditions cannot be apprehended, how much less so that which is without causes and conditions?
These four are all conceptual constructions and speculative reckonings; therefore, they must be refuted.
Question:
The Buddha-dharma universally states that all things arise through the combination of causes and conditions; why, then, is "co-arising" refuted?
Answer:
Because there is a fixed attachment to it, it too must be refuted.
Once the four types of grasping have been refuted, the four types of teaching are free from fault.

Regarding "that which is refuted by the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*," the treatise states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without cause; therefore, it is said that there is no arising."
Since Nāgārjuna has already refuted [these views], how could one still hold the four kinds of attachments as before?
Is this not merely further false speech? Regarding the sixty-two views:

[the views that] "the self is large and form is small," or "form is large and the self is small"; that "form is the self," or "the self is apart from form"—the same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*). Including the five aggregates across the three periods of time, these total sixty.
Since they do not depart from existence and non-existence, all sixty-two views are subsumed under the category of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

When the four views arise regarding objects and cognition, in reality all eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) arise together; it is merely for the sake of brevity that extreme views and the three types of feeling are mentioned.

If one were to discuss this fully: to cling to any single phrase, thinking, "I understand and know this Dharma," and thereby conceiving a self within the Dharma is the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). To cling to the first three or two phrases is to fall into the extreme of existence; to cling to the second four or two phrases is to fall into the extreme of non-existence. These are subsumed within the sixty-two views, which constitute the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Such false attachments that do not accord with reason constitute wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To cling to this as real and conceive of it as *nirvāṇa* constitutes the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To falsely claim this as the path and to proceed by relying upon it constitutes the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Regarding the three types of suffering resulting from theft: pleasant sensations involve the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); painful sensations involve the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); and sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant involve the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

As for the phrase "pleasant sensations lead to craving," it means that one clings to a particular object and cognition as being correct; if others praise it, the mind becomes attached and gives rise to joy, experiencing mental pleasure—this is the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*).
Regarding painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*): if others act in opposition, one gives rise to anger and aversion, and the mind suffers; this is the latent tendency of hatred (*dveṣānuśaya*).

Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling: if one is neither reviled nor praised, one remains in the state of the latent tendency of delusion (*mohānuśaya*) with equal parts, and is likewise subsumed within the three latent tendencies.

Furthermore, my understanding of this object and wisdom is not understood by others; because they take pride in their own attachments and act with arrogance toward me, this is the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*).
Since they grasp this as being correct, although they do not doubt it now, they will surely come to have great doubt later; this is the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
Thus, these ten proclivities (daśa-anuśaya) are clearly present, all arising from the objects and cognitions to which one clings.
When these are applied across the three realms and the four noble truths, there are eighty-eight proclivities.
When one contemplates the pervasive afflictions across the three realms, there are ninety-eight *anuśayas*.

Now, regarding the five sharp [afflictions], only *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (extreme views) is briefly cited; regarding the five dull [afflictions], only the four divisions are briefly clarified. To speak from the essential point: because the objects and cognitions of these four categories all fall into one-sided extremes, and because the three types of sensation arise based on what is grasped therein, their characteristics are easy to perceive; therefore, they are explained here first.

As discussed in detail above, there are ninety-eight [defilements] in total; therefore, the subsequent text states: "To know that within each phrase there are ninety-eight *anuśayas* is called 'recognizing the disease.

Regarding the "eighty-four thousand afflictions" (*kleśas*), the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, based on the *Daśānuśaya-sūtra*, takes the ten [root] defilements—beginning with greed and ending with the clinging to precepts—as the foundation. That is to say, for each of these ten, from greed through the clinging to precepts, there are nine [subdivisions] plus one latent tendency (*anuśaya*), which together constitute ten.
Ten becomes one hundred; with equal divisions of the preceding and succeeding parts, each being one hundred, they become three hundred.

Taking the original one hundred as the basis, within the two hundred of the preceding and succeeding parts, ten further are used as the means (*upāya*) for each, whereby the two hundred become two thousand one hundred.

Approximately five classes of sentient beings are distinguished—namely, those with excessive greed, excessive anger, excessive delusion, attachment to self, and discursive thought—with two thousand one hundred individuals in each of these five categories, totaling ten thousand five hundred.
When these are further correlated with whether they have arisen or have not yet arisen, they constitute twenty-one thousand.
Furthermore, when these are correlated with greed, hatred, delusion, and the equal portion (sādhāraṇa), each of these four categories contains twenty-one thousand, resulting in eighty-four thousand.
Regarding the current statement that "it is extracted from the *Caturvarga*," although the number of delusions is vast, they are all fully subsumed within these four categories.
As for "ultimate emptiness and quiescence," it is because there are no four attachments.
"Non-reliance" refers to the state of emptiness and stillness.
The intent of the question is: since the principle is already empty and still, for what reason do there exist the paths, cessation, causes, and effects?
The meaning of the answer is this: merely to cognize suffering and its origin, without being obstructed by the four attachments, is called the Truth of the Path.
That which is empty and quiescent as the object of focus is the Truth of Cessation.
The passage "knowing the four" below demonstrates the characteristics of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Regarding "the defiled five aggregates," the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) clarifies nine types of the five aggregates:

1. The physical and mental elements of a single lifetime are called "retribution" (*vipāka*); 2. Neutral perceptions and sensations are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*); 3. The arising of views and the arising of craving are called the "two defilements"; 4. The wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are divided into two; 5. Transformations and manifestations are called "artistry" (*śailpasthānika*); 6. Those possessing the three roots of goodness are called "expedient means" (*upāya*); 7. The four fruits [of the path] are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
Now, because views and craving arise toward objects and consciousness, they are called "defiled.
To not accept [them] means to contemplate that sensation is suffering.
The other two [aggregates] are omitted for brevity.
Regarding "the factors of the path, etc.," the term "etc. includes the three, four, two, five, seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.
The phrase "and again, correct" below indicates the characteristics of the truth of cessation.

Taking that which is capable of contemplation as the Buddha, that which is contemplated as the Dharma, and the non-duality of object and contemplation as the Sangha—these three meanings within a single mind constitute the Three Jewels of Identical Substance.
"Awakening and comprehending" refers to the three contemplations that can be practiced;
"the four attachments" refers to the delusive afflictions to be eliminated;
and "dharma-nature" refers to the three truths that are the objects of contemplation.
Because the object and the contemplation are non-dual, they are said to be "harmoniously integrated.

Furthermore, the reason the Truth of Cessation is presented within the context of right effort is that, when the factors of enlightenment (mārga-aṅga) are categorized by stage, right effort corresponds to the stage of the inner ordinary person (pṛthagjana) of the Hīnayāna.
Applying the small to the great, one realizes the cessation [of suffering] through the perfecting of the six sense faculties.

Regarding the phrase "the mind that abides nowhere" and so forth: it means that the Great Sage has no fourfold attachments internally, while externally he accords with the conditions of sentient beings to enable them to obtain the four benefits, thereby explaining the distinction between the object and the wisdom.

This means that if a person delights in hearing that objects and cognition arise spontaneously, one explains that the object is its own object and the cognition is its own cognition, in order to satisfy their longing.
Alternatively, for those who should hear about the arising of wholesome states, or for those who must break through delusions, one teaches accordingly.
Some attain enlightenment upon hearing [the teaching]; others likewise have no other cause for it.
Therefore, what is elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras—whether regarding objects or wisdom—does not transcend the "self" and its equivalents.
Among those listed by name, the objects and wisdom of the four teachings all accord with the four *siddhāntas*.
Only the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) is specifically so named because, at the stage of emerging into the provisional, it primarily employs the four *siddhāntas* to transform others.
The designation "Perfect" (Yuan) as "inconceivable" (bùsīyì) reveals that the three preceding teachings are all "conceivable" (sīyì).

However, since the fourfold objects and wisdoms collectively explain the two characters "Contemplating the World" (guānshì), one should anticipate their distinctions so that they may be easily understood when the text is reached.

The former two take the six realms and three types of worlds arising from the mind as their object, yet there is a distinction between them in terms of whether wisdom possesses substantiality or is analytically deconstructed.
The Separate Teaching takes the ten realms and three types of worlds arising from the mind as its object, employing sequential wisdom.
The Perfect Teaching takes the ten realms and the three types of worlds as its object, employing the threefold wisdom of the one mind.

Regarding the statement "all dharmas arise from conditions," it means that the objects of cognition and the wisdom that cognizes them, as well as their causal conditions, are all substantially real; this is the "emptiness through analysis" (*prabheda-śūnyatā*).
"Merely having a name" means that when a jar has been broken or a head has been severed, there remains only the designation "jar" or "head," while the actual substance no longer exists.
This analogy is derived from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
"These characters do not abide" refers to the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
"Nor do they not abide" refers to the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma-eye" and so forth, this refers to the manifestation of the provisional [world] through the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), wherein the objects and wisdom of the Four Teachings and the Four *Siddhāntas* are expounded.
Regarding the phrase "although there is neither object nor wisdom," phenomena are created from the mind; the entire Dharma is the mind itself.
The mind is fundamentally non-existent; how then could all phenomena be established?
Though they do not exist, they appear to exist; the three thousand worlds are manifest.
Since beginningless time there has been non-awakening; while the principle is inherently complete, sentient emotions remain deluded.

Now that one has awakened to this understanding, one knows that the mind itself is not separate from the observing faculty, yet there is nothing else to be illuminated; nevertheless, within the single mind, one forcibly distinguishes between object and wisdom—hence it is said, "yet they are discussed."
Regarding the phrase "The Sūtra says," "object" refers to that which is observed, and "illumination" refers to that which observes.
Since the subject and object are of one suchness, both are described as "inconceivable.
As for the term "intending to emulate," the Great Master remains humble, expressing that he has no exclusive attachment.
"Having long since eliminated the four attachments" means that one has attained the mind of non-abiding.

Regarding "compassion" and so forth, these are directed toward those with partial or perfect capacities and manifest as the forms of the four teachings; therefore, the preceding explanation of the names was based on the four types of objects and wisdom.
The phrase "Thus, the Sūtra" below introduces a scriptural citation as proof.
In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Śāriputra asks the goddess:
"In which of the three vehicles do you seek to aspire?"
The deva said:
"Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the śrāvakas, I am a śrāvaka.
Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas, I am a pratyekabuddha."
"Because I transform sentient beings through great compassion, I am for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
Since both Avalokiteśvara and the goddess share the same reality, they can serve as mutual testimony.
In the detailed explanation, if one follows the conventional order of names, one should first clarify the wisdom of contemplation and subsequently distinguish the mundane objects.

If it is more convenient to explain according to the meaning, one first clarifies the worldly objects and subsequently distinguishes the contemplative wisdom; for one can discuss contemplation based on the prior existence of an object that can be apprehended—if no object existed, what would there be to contemplate?
For example, it is like a mirror and a drum, which reflect and strike one another from behind.
Here, for the sake of convenience in exposition, the object is mentioned first, followed by the wisdom.

Regarding "the three truths and the three objects," the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) clarifies that the rational nature is one; it is called a "truth" (*satya*) in relation to cessation (*śamatha*), and an "object" (*viṣaya*) in relation to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
What is elucidated in various texts is that the truths are themselves the objects; it is not said that there is a distinction between the two.
Now, I shall follow this same principle. Why is this so?
This is because various texts merely speak of the "three contemplations" (sanzhuan) without discussing the "three cessations" (san zhi).
Furthermore, the practice gates of cessation and contemplation (zhiguan) will now be presented in detail.
From the phrase "The first cause" onwards, the names are enumerated.

Regarding the phrase "these three objects": it means that these three objects are neither one nor three; they exist solely within a single thought-moment, universally encompassing all phenomena, wherein the three are without distinction and mutually interfuse with one another.

It is only because the mind is deluded that one cannot awaken to this; thus, within the dharmas that are inherently unbound, one forcibly creates fetters, asserting distinctions between sentient and insentient beings, and between phenomena and their underlying principle.

Within the dharma of non-liberation, one falsely seeks liberation; consequently, one comes to loathe suffering and delight in pleasure, abandons existence to enter emptiness, and departs from the two extremes to seek the Middle Way. Thus, there arise the distinctions between the birth-and-death of ordinary beings and the objects and wisdom of the three teachings. Therefore, it is said: "That which is observed by wisdom constitutes four."

Regarding the four kinds of contemplation, the Sūtra states: "By contemplating with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; by contemplating with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; by contemplating with superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a bodhisattva; and by contemplating with the most superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a Buddha."
Now, the present treatise explains the meaning by correlating it with the four teachings (*catuḥśāsana*).
Since the Śrāvaka is the Hīnayāna Piṭaka and represents the most inferior teaching, Śrāvaka-bodhi is precisely the Teaching of the Piṭaka (*piṭaka-śāsana*);
the Pratyekabuddha is the Middle Vehicle of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānya-śāsana*), situated between the Piṭaka and the Distinct Teaching (*prātibheda-śāsana*).
The Bodhisattva vehicle is the distinct teaching (biete jiao) of the Supreme Vehicle (shangsheng), which still stands above the common teaching (tongjiao);
the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) further stands above the distinct teaching, and is therefore called "supreme among the supreme" (shangshang).
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra* can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "Ultimately, these are the realms of the three truths": although the faculties may be partial or complete, leading to delusion regarding four realms, when one discusses the fundamental principle, the three truths are eternally integrated.

Regarding the phrase "opened into two contemplations": this means that both the preceding *pitaka* (Treasury) and the *pratyekabuddha* (Individual) contemplations equally contemplate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

In the section beginning with "Answer," although conventional truth is the same for both, they are divided into two distinct categories because the *pitaka* perceives coarse characteristics while the *pratyekabuddha* perceives subtle characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "the truth is also shallow or deep": the first three fruits are shallow because they involve partial realization (*darśana-bhāga*), while the fourth fruit is deep because it is ultimate.
Furthermore, they are mutually shallow and deep.
Since two types of conventional truth—the coarse and the subtle—have been distinguished, there must likewise be two levels of ultimate truth: the shallow and the deep.
Regarding the phrase "the principle is non-dual": although there are differences in the depth of insight, the true emptiness is but one.
Since this is the case for the partial truth, it should be understood by analogy for the middle truth as well.

This terminology of "shallow" and "deep" cannot be explained away by applying the "repeated truth" (*punar-satya*) of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), because the text states, "the principle is non-dual"; if one were to rely on the repeated truth, it would clearly be dual.
Thus, one should know that the intent of the responses each follows its respective category.
Regarding the phrase "observing equally" (*samanupaśyanā*) and so forth, it should be understood as collectively concluding the preceding enumeration.
Previously, based on the protection of self and others and so forth, combining the subject and object, there were seventy-eight [categories].
Now, if we examine this through the contemplative methods of the four teachings, there are three hundred and twelve petitions.

Regarding the passage "Next, clarifying wisdom" (*zhìmíng zhì*) and below: as for the two dharmas of object (*viṣaya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), they are undivided yet divided. Therefore, the previous explanation of the object was clarified in contrast to wisdom; now, the explanation of wisdom is again stated in reference to the object. Thus we know that the object is not manifest without wisdom, and wisdom is not established without the object. Although their meanings follow one another, the text has both lateral and primary emphases.
"Contemplating causes and conditions" below indicates the wisdom of the Tripitaka (Tripiṭaka-jñāna).
"Contemplating the emptiness of causes and conditions" indicates the wisdom of the Shared [Vehicle] (Sādhāraṇa-jñāna).
Regarding "contemplation of the two truths": the provisional is the false conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while emptiness is the verified ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Now, wishing to leave the mundane world and return to the truth, one speaks of "contemplation" (*guan*).

Since emptiness and the provisional are the means for entering emptiness, one must first contemplate the provisional to realize its falsity and thereby attain union with the true; thus, it is called the contemplation of the two truths.
Below the phrase "Emerging into the Provisional" (*chujia*), the distinct wisdom is designated.
Because it emerges from emptiness, it is called "emerging into the provisional.
Because it enters within the provisional, it is also termed "entering the provisional."
Therefore, the two names "Entering" and "Exiting" are established interchangeably across various texts.
Although there are three distinct contemplations, the "contemplation of the provisional" is taken as the primary one.
As for the "contemplation of equality," it is termed "equality" in relation to what preceded it.
Previously, the provisional was refuted by means of emptiness; now, emptiness is refuted by means of the provisional. Since the refutation of their functions is equal, it is called "equality.
Below the term "Middle Way," the perfect wisdom is indicated.

Although the three contemplations are unified within a single mind, they are designated by their most prominent feature; thus, the Middle Way is pointed out, and all three are called "contemplation" (guan) and further termed "wisdom" (zhi).
When discussed in general terms, the meanings of contemplation and wisdom are one and the same;
yet when distinguished individually, they are divided into two categories: cause and effect.
The phrase "worldly wisdom" (*loka-jñāna*) below serves to censure ordinary people.
Since both ordinary people and non-Buddhists possess this kind of wisdom, yet fail to transcend birth and death and remain unmoved by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is described as "worldly wisdom."
Regarding the phrase "merely having a name": because this worldly wisdom is deceptive and unreal, it possesses only the designation of "wisdom" but lacks its actual substance.
Therefore, it was previously stated that it is "also called the wisdom of names."
Regarding the phrase "commonly used by both ordinary beings and sages": this means that ordinary beings employ this wisdom to attain the four dhyānas and eight samāpattis.
There are two different types of sages:
those liberated through wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) solely by employing untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
Those who are liberated in both ways employ both types of wisdom; at the time of severing afflictions, they employ one or the other as the occasion requires.
Therefore, it is said that "both ordinary beings and sages employ them universally.
Since these wisdoms are equally possessed by both ordinary beings and sages, it was previously stated that they are also called "equalizing wisdom" (*samvṛti-jñāna*).
The section beginning with "But this" concludes the refutation.
The section beginning with "Bodhisattva" reveals the Bodhisattva.
The phrase "In this contemplation" refers to mundane wisdom (*loka-jñāna*).

Since one has not yet severed the afflictions, one merely employs mundane wisdom to contemplate impermanence and cultivate the six perfections; by perfecting this resolute understanding, one will ultimately transcend birth and death.
"Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity" refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).

Because of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one bestows happiness; because of compassion (*karuṇā*), one removes suffering; because of seeing others free from suffering and attaining happiness, one feels sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and because one does not seek any reward for one's kindness, one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Since these four are applied equally toward both enemies and kin without discrimination, they are called the "four immeasurables" (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
"Endowed with all dharmas" refers to the complete cultivation of the ten thousand practices, namely the six perfections and the four immeasurables.

"The thirty-four minds" refers to the eight patiences and eight knowledges which eliminate the afflictions of the path of seeing, and the nine paths of non-interruption and nine paths of liberation which eliminate the afflictions of the path of cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "such as Kātyāyanīputra," this refers to the *Śāstra* (Commentary) citing Kātyāyanīputra’s clarification of the meaning of a bodhisattva.
Śākyamuni was formerly a potter who, encountering a previous Śākyamuni Buddha, resolved to attain bodhicitta and practiced the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Regarding "The Contemplation of the Threefold Treasury’s Realm and Wisdom, Avalokiteśvara": the Bodhisattva has personally subdued the six obscurations and permeates all things with a heart of compassion; thus, when sentient beings invoke his name, he is immediately able to liberate them from suffering.

Practicing the six perfections oneself and permeating all things with a mind of loving-kindness, one is able to manifest before those who are ready to be saved, enabling them to attain peace and happiness.

Regarding the phrase "although practicing in emptiness," etc.: from the stage of the Thin Ground (mṛdubhūmi), the Bodhisattva trains in the playful exercise of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and extensively cultivates the contemplation of the conventional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*); upon reaching the eighth ground, they emerge from the conventional, and for this reason, it is said that they do not abide in emptiness.
“Initial mind” refers to the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase “becoming like a Buddha,” it means that those who are received [into this teaching] are able to shatter ignorance; once ignorance is shattered, they become like those who have attained the Buddha-ground because they equally realize the eight aspects of enlightenment—therefore, they are said to be “like” [a Buddha].

Regarding the phrase "different from the Shared Teaching" and so forth: the distinct person (biperson) breaks through emptiness to emerge into the provisional, whereas the person of the Shared Teaching emerges into the provisional from within emptiness; the former sustains habitual tendencies to moisten rebirth, knowing that emptiness is not empty.
In the sixth and seventh abodes, one shatters emptiness to emerge into the provisional;
this refers to the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). "Dust-like sands" refers to the phenomena that are the objects of delusion;
"ignorance" refers to the mind that performs the delusion.

The *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states: "In the Ten Abodes, one eliminates the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*), and further eliminates the superior grade of 'dust-like sand' (*rajas*) afflictions beyond the realms.
Among the Ten Practices, there is the middle grade; among the Ten Transferences, the inferior grade. The present treatise concerns the middle grade.

Regarding "the fulfillment of practice": according to the distinct teaching (*bye-brag-pa'i bstan-pa*, *vyatireka-śāsana*) as elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras, the stage immediately preceding Equal Enlightenment (*mnyam-par-rdzogs-pa'i byang-chub*, *samabhisambodhi*) may either exist or not exist.
Here, speaking from the perspective of its non-existence, it is said that "the practice of the ten stages is fulfilled."

Regarding "contemplation that accords with principle": even the distinct sequential contemplations do not accord with principle; it can be understood that the analytical and substantial methods of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings likewise do not accord with it.
The perfect fusion of the three truths is the primordial nature of reality itself; because one contemplates in accordance with this nature, it is called "accordance with principle."
The phrase "Since the principle... and below indicates the characteristics that accord with the principle.
Regarding "From the beginning to the end": "the beginning" refers to the name; practicing contemplation based on understanding is called the "Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara by Name."
The "subsequent" refers to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), wherein the principle is ultimately revealed; this is called the "Ultimate Avalokiteśvara.
Although the five stages differ in their positions, the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*) remains a single unity.
Regarding the phrase "perfectly eliminating the five abodes," it means that the three delusions are simultaneously shattered.
Question:
Since both categories of delusions have already been eliminated prior to the stage of the Ten Faiths, why is it said that the five abodes are completely removed?
Answer:
Through the perfect contemplation of the nature of mind, coarse defilements are naturally removed; thus, the four foundations of mindfulness are likened to refining iron.
Therefore, through perfect contemplation, the first stage (Prathamābhūmi) can be attained within a single lifetime.
If one follows the gradual path, even if two delusions are eliminated first during a single lifetime such that they are not experienced in sequence, it still constitutes a gradual path.

Whether it be the Perfect [Vehicle] connecting with the Separate, the Separate connecting with the Perfect, or resolving the Perfect while practicing gradually—in all these cases, if the two delusions are eliminated first, none of them accord with our present intention.
The present text specifically addresses practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle], and therefore speaks of "perfect eradication.
Regarding the phrase "Avalokiteśvara of Wondrous Enlightenment," a question is raised:
Since Avalokiteśvara is a being on the causal stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), why is he explained here in terms of the ultimate fruit of Wondrous Enlightenment?
Answer:
The *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi Sūtra* states: "This Bodhisattva has already attained perfect enlightenment; his name is Buddha Righteous Dharma Radiance (*Saddharmaprabhāsa*).
The *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa Sūtra* states: "He shall next succeed to the position of the Regent, and shall be called Universal Radiance Merit (*Samantaprabhā-guṇa*)."
Such are its fundamental and manifest aspects.
Interpreted according to the ultimate meaning, there should be no error in principle.
Question:
It may be so regarding its specific names;
but what is its general designation?
Answer:
Although the text is not explicit, there is this interpretation by precedent, referring to those from the "name-designation bodhisattva" up to the "ultimate bodhisattva.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among sentient beings, the unsurpassed is the Buddha."

How much more so for Bodhisattvas and sentient beings! While there are differences between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms, the name applies even to the ultimate fruit; the textual meaning lies herein.
Regarding the phrase "these three knowledges," together with mundane knowledge there are four; however, because mundane knowledge is the object [of cognition], only three are mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "also corresponding to the five eyes": since the three types of wisdom are categorized according to the four teachings, the same applies to the five eyes.

The two eyes—the flesh eye and the divine eye—illuminate coarse and subtle phenomena; both are mundane wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and serve as the basis for all meditative contemplations, which corresponds to the first line of the verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
In the teachings of the *Pitaka*, Avalokiteśvara does not sever the afflictions; therefore, he is described solely in terms of the two eyes of worldly knowledge.

If one considers the perspective of the Two Vehicles, from this point they enter the contemplation of analytical dharma (*vibhajya-dharma-vipaśyanā*), and by severing delusions, they also attain the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

Furthermore, although a Bodhisattva attains the five supernormal powers and acquires the Dharma-eye during the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas and one hundred kalpas— thereby discerning the faculties and natures of sentient beings to bring them to maturity—
if viewed from the perspective of the distinct teaching (biejiao), these are designated merely as "worldly wisdom" and the "two eyes."
The general [perspective] pertains solely to the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), while the specific pertains solely to the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); the meaning is likewise.
"Illuminating the Truth" refers to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); thus, in contrast to the wisdom-eye, it corresponds to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*).
"Shining upon the provisional" refers to the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā); thus, in contrast to the "Dharma-eye," this constitutes the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna).
"Medicine" refers to the Truths of the Path and Cessation.
"Illness" refers to the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
